**Setup.** A *billiards table* is a bounded polygon whose corners are *pockets*. A trajectory $P(t)$ is *degenerate* if $P(t)$ is a pocket for some $t>0$, and *periodic* if there is a constant $C>0$ with $P(t+C)=P(t)$ for all $t$ (the clock may also be run backwards, so $P(t)$ is defined for $t<0$ too); the smallest such $C$ is the *period*. The *combinatorial period* of a periodic trajectory is the number of times it hits an edge during one period (the same edge, or even the same point, may be hit several times and each hit is counted).

An *$n$-billiards table* is a regular $n$-gon with unit side length and pockets at all corners, placed so that its bottom-most edge (the *base*) lies on the positive $x$-axis with its left end at the origin $O$. Angles of directions are measured counterclockwise from the base.

On the $3$-billiards table (the equilateral triangle with unit sides), a ball starts at the midpoint of the base, moving at an angle $\theta$ above the base, as in the figure. It bounces off the right side, then the left side, then the base, and then goes straight into the top pocket (degenerate trajectory). Compute $\tan\theta$ as an exact expression.

A *simple billiards table* is a convex polygon with pockets at its corners. You may use the following theorem.

**Theorem.** For any simple billiards table, if a line segment starts at a point $P_1$ on an edge $e_1$ and ends at a point $P_2$ on an edge $e_2$, with $P_1,P_2$ not pockets, then there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $\overline{P_1P_2}$ is translated perpendicular to its direction by any $t<\epsilon$ and extended/cropped to a segment $\overline{P_1^tP_2^t}$ with $P_1^t$ on $e_1$ and $P_2^t$ on $e_2$, the line $\overline{P_1^tP_2^t}$ does not contain a pocket.
